speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
subsubtopic: STATEMENT AS TO COURSE TO BE FOLLOWED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the question raised about the business of the house by hon. members opposite on Friday, I should like to make a brief statement which I hope will leave no doubt in the mind of any hon. member about the position of the government in asking at this time for one month's interim supply. Just before the house adjourned on Friday, I stated that the government could not suggest adjourning after having obtained only one month's supply. If one month's supply is granted at the present time, it would be our intention to proceed with the business of the session in the normal way, and before the end of June to ask for a further grant of interim supply and continue the session. In arranging the order of business the government would, as usual, consult hon. members opposite as to the most convenient way of bringing forward matters for debate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 24 last, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fair-clough) asked about an increase in working hours for certain security guards employed by the defence research board. I take it that her reference was to a small number of security guards employed by the defence research board at headquarters and in the Daly annex building.
Under the National Defence Act employees of the board do not come under the Civil Service Act, but whenever their working conditions run parallel to civil service regulations, the board can extend to such employees benefits accruing to civil servants of similar classifications.
The guards referred to by the hon. lady are classified by the board as watchmen, and civil servants in the classification of watchmen or security supervisors are required under present regulations to work a 48-hour week.
Consequently, when new civil service rates of pay were being worked out recently, the board undertook to readjust the working conditions of these watchmen to the same basis as that for watchmen in other government establishments in this area. This meant an increase in pay as from April 1 last and

this was followed by an adjustment of shifts to bring these employees on to a 48-hour week.

subtopic: DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a supplementary question to the minister. Is it not true that the increase in pay which they received was merely the statutory increase or the regular increase which was given to all civil servants at that time? Despite this fact, I understand that these people had their work week increased from I think 42-J hours to 48 hours for which additional time they received no compensation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: That is true, Mr. Speaker, and I would make two observations about it. One is that these people are not under the civil service commission and therefore are not in that sense civil servants. The second point is that we are hopeful we will be able to obtain a civil service classification for watchmen more suitable than the present classification which would make up for some of the discrepancy.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the request for interim supply usually raises no question because of the undertaking that is given by the Minister of Finance in the ordinary course of events in terms similar to those which have been stated today. Naturally there has been a good deal of speculation as to what would happen at this time in view of the circumstances in which we find ourselves. Normally there is no question raised. In fact I believe that there has been only one instance in the history of the House of Commons where there has been any delay and it would appear that the delay on that occasion was through inadvertence rather than for any other reason.
However, the circumstances in this case are not normal. We have indicated clearly that so far as we are concerned our attitude toward the management of the business of the country by the government has not in any way been changed by the disposition of the debate which was before us. I hope we have made it equally clear that the lack of confidence we expressed in the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker was not something to be disposed of by the mere passage of the measure which had been under consideration at the time we were called upon to express that lack of confidence.
The situation with which we are confronted is not going to be affected during the course of the present parliament by a mere passage of time. The things that have occurred are too fundamental in their effect upon our parliamentary system to be forgotten. This is not a case of letting bygones be bygones. To our great regret, the relationship of the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker has become inconsistent with our traditions in this house, so far as their relationship with the full membership of the house is concerned. It is for that reason that we would still express the hope that the government would have the courage to follow the honourable course and to dissolve this parliament and permit the early election of a new parliament which would be in harmony with the sentiments of the people of Canada, who now have knowledge of the whole situation.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I should hope that we should have the assurance that, after the appropriate disposition of business in this house, the Prime Minister would take the constitutional steps to obtain dissolution and permit the people to express their opinion on what has happened here. I leave that request before the Prime Minister. I believe it is a request which in no way becomes diminished in its force by lapse of time. On the contrary, each day that passes gives greater force to the need for the expression of that opinion by our people.
In the meantime, however, we are now called upon to deal with the motion for interim supply. What has happened here is typical of the way in which the business of this country is being done. It is now June 11; the last interim supply motion provided supply until May 31. It is in keeping with the attitude of this government to the house and to the people of Canada that it should now come before us on June 11 to ask that there be further funds advanced to meet the requirements, which are now extremely urgent.
It is altogether likely that the cheques have already been prepared and are ready to be sent out for the payments due on June 15. That is the way in which this house has become accustomed to be treated by this government. It should be remembered, however, that it is the people of Canada that are being treated in this way. This is typical of the way in which time limits are set and the ordinary opportunities to examine curtailed by the severe restriction of time.
It is only natural that there should have been discussion in the press and elsewhere as to what would happen to the very large number of civil servants, members of the armed forces and others whose cheques are dependent upon the voting of interim supply. In waiting until June 11 to present this motion for interim supply, the government showed scant concern for the civil servants, the members of the armed forces or others who work for pay. Everything has been subordinated to the determination of the government to ram the pipe line bill down the throats of this parliament and the people of Canada. Everything else has been set aside, no matter how urgent or important it was. Merely one example in addition to what we now have before us will serve to indicate the way that all other important business has been held in a state of suspense by the compelling demand of this government that they meet a time limit set by the

company which has received such concern and consideration from the government during the past weeks.
That other subject is national defence. Nearly half the money that is collected from the taxpayers of Canada goes either directly or indirectly into the vitally important requirements of national defence. It is now more than five months since this session began on January 10 and there has been no discussion of any kind of national defence. During the current sessions of the various legislative bodies of Britain, the United States and Russia, as well as other countries whose activities are important at this time, there has been an examination of national defence and there has been an extensive reorganization of the national defence forces.
As early as December 21 the members of the House of Commons in Britain were informed regarding the nature of the reorganization that was to take place there, including a reduction of the armed forces, a streamlining of the organization and a general modernization of the whole concept of national defence. The same has taken place in the United States where sweeping reorganization has taken place for the strengthening and improving of their defence forces with a smaller number of men. More recently still the same thing has taken place in Russia. So far as we are concerned, this subject has not been before us and the item for national defence has not even been called yet as one of the items that could be brought before the house for discussion in the consideration of estimates.
That is typical of the way that the government has been marking time while it sought by every device first to bring its own members into line and then to impose the will of the government upon this house. There might be many reasons for us to indicate our very strong conviction that the government no longer has any reason to be offered evidence of confidence by the members of this house or the people of Canada. However, the fact remains that what is now before us is the provision of one-twelfth of the amount of money that will be required in any event. We have the assurance of the Prime Minister that business is going to proceed in its ordinary way and that we will have the opportunity to examine the estimates as we should.
The reason I asked the questions I did on Thursday and on Friday was that there were reports coming from what would ordinarily be regarded as very reliable sources to the effect that there was to be an adjournment during the summer months. We certainly would not have agreed to any suspension of the activities of this house at a time when
Interim Supply
such important business as national defence, national health and other matters of that kind were to be discussed here in the House of Commons. All the important departments that are still to be brought before the house should be examined with the utmost care.
We now have the answer we sought last week, and are told that the business will proceed. In any event we had no thought, and we have no thought, of permitting the civil servants, the members of the armed forces and others to be made the victims of this government's misconduct. We shall, therefore, consent in the usual way to interim supply on the basis of the assurance given by the Minister of Finance and on the basis of the assurance given by the Prime Minister that the business of this house will proceed to its termination in the usual way without interruption.
I hope that the future business of this session, for whatever length of time it may last, will be conducted on a more businesslike basis. I hope that when any request is going to be made which calls for the consideration of supply or other matters, it will be brought forward in time to consider it without being confronted with deadlines which would limit in any way the normal process of debate.
Before I conclude these remarks, Mr. Chairman, may I express the hope that the government will not again cause the concern, and very natural concern, in the minds of the civil servants, members of the armed forces and others which they have aroused on this occasion by the way in which they forgot the interests of these people and subordinated their duty to these public servants in the way that they have on this occasion, particularly for the purpose for which it was done. I would hope that we will have ample opportunity to deal with every item in the same way that we have on other occasions in the past. I would hope that there would be no thought in the minds of civil servants that the sword of Damocles is hanging over their heads and that they must depend on the whims of this government for adequate consideration of their requirements as they have at this time.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have indicated that we shall follow the course that we would follow ordinarily. We shall look forward to an early opportunity to deal with the important items that require consideration, and we shall proceed as rapidly as possible to permit interim supply to be adopted. I repeat my request however, that as we do this we recall that this is merely one more example of the way in which the government has disregarded the rights of parliament, the rights of civil servants and others employed by the government, and above all the rights of the people

Interim Supply
of Canada. It is hoped that the government will recognize the situation with which we are now confronted in this house and will not impose upon the Speaker and Deputy Speaker, a task with which they should not be confronted because of the actions of the government. I do hope the government will proceed with the business, and at the same time give us the assurance that this whole unhappy atmosphere will be cleared up by the constitutional procedure that can be followed, and that the people of Canada will have the right to choose the kind of parliament they want.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
It is still our view, Mr. Chairman, that there is one honourable way in which this government can obtain the supply that is necessary in order to meet civil servants' salaries and other payments due on Friday of this week. This honourable way has been suggested by the Leader of the Opposition, namely that the government should indicate to the house its readiness to dissolve this parliament at an early date and call a general election. If that proposal were made to this house we would have no hesitation in granting whatever number of months' interim supply is necessary to carry on the business of government until a new parliament should meet.
Let me say again, Mr. Chairman, that this group still feels that the government of the day has lost the confidence of the people of this country. It may be possible for the government still to muster a majority vote in the House of Commons, which was elected nearly three years ago. We believe, however, that particularly as a result of what has been done to parliament in recent weeks, this government does not possess the confidence of the people of Canada. Because it does not possess that confidence, a fact which arises because of its own actions in parliament, we say that the government does not have the moral authority to come before parliament today and ask interim supply in the normal way; in other words, to ask parliament to allow it to carry on just as if nothing had happened.
Supply has ended. The civil servants must be paid. Other bills must be met. These very necessities add, we feel, to the insistence that what we should be told at this time by the government is that it is prepared to dissolve this parliament and call a general election. We would be quite prepared for the date of dissolution to be put off whatever number of weeks might be necessary for such important business as is before parliament to be concluded, and indeed for the estimates to be concluded in the normal

way. But we feel very strongly that this government does not possess the moral authority, nor does this parliament possess the authority necessary to carry on, in view of what has been done to it by the government, and dissolution is the only answer to the situation.
I quite understand the conclusion to which the Leader of the Opposition has come, but I confess that it is not in my heart to give such ready consent, in terms of letting things go through quickly, to a government that has done to parliament what this House of Commons has suffered during the past few weeks. What parliament does with the request of the government will, of course, be up to the members of this house. But I repeat that in our view the government does not have the moral authority to make the request that has been presented to us. Actually the Prime Minister and the government should reconsider the making of this request. It is obvious the government is hoping that in some way we will let bygones be bygones and that in some way time will heal the wounds, and the government will be enabled to rehabilitate its position before it has to go to the people of this country. We do not think that is the honourable way to deal with this situation. We think that moral standards call for something much better than that.
So far as the relationship between the House of Commons and the government is concerned I am reminded of what Durell has to say in his book "Parliamentary Grants", on page 4, where I read:
It is, indeed, ultimately to the power of the purse, to its power to bring the whole executive machinery of the country to a standstill, that the House of Commons owes its control over the executive. That is the fountain and origin of its historical victories over the other organs of the state; and since that power was recognized and confirmed towards the end of the 17th century, the House of Commons has remained, whether reformed or unreformed, whether corrupt or incorrupt, the chief arbiter of the national destinies.
That is the position this House of Commons is in this afternoon. We have an executive in whom we believe the people of Canada have no confidence, making a request to us, which is more than a request just for the salaries of civil servants, but rather is a request that we permit this government to carry on in the normal way. Out of concern for the position of civil servants and in view of the position that the Leader of the Opposition has taken, we may have to grant such supply as is necessary to pay those salaries. In my own mind I am not sure just what is the right thing for an opposition to do in a situation like this,

particularly after what the Leader of the Opposition has said, but I say, Mr. Chairman, the granting of interim supply will be done, if it is done at all, under protest, with this declaration which I make to the government: You are asking something that you have no moral authority to request from a free Canadian parliament.
Despite what the Prime Minister said on Friday about civil servants and others who should not be called upon to suffer because of party warfare, I assert, Mr. Chairman, that the issue is not whether civil servants are to receive their salaries. Incidentally, 'because in my remarks I seem to be referring to civil servants only and not to those of the armed forces, I may say that I have done that because it is my understanding that the nature of the national defence estimates is such that there is plenty of money for the paying of the armed forces. As hon. members know, the national defence estimates consist mainly of one large item for something over $1,700 million, and in that item there are included subitems for wages and salaries and also items for ships, guns, planes, tanks and ammunition. Already the government has one-sixth of that total sum. Because some of those other things such as ships, guns and planes have not been purchased there is enough money there, so I understand, for the armed forces to be paid at the middle of this month. Therefore, if there is concern at all about the meeting of salaries this week it is only with respect to the civil servants. But, may I say, Mr. Chairman, that in our view the issue is not civil servants' salaries. This government has no right to claim that that is the issue.
On May 25 when the government's chief concern was in getting its pipe line bill through parliament I asked the Minister of Finance this question, as recorded at page 4325 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. When does the minister intend to ask the house for further interim supply?
On behalf of this government that is now so concerned that it is asking parliament to help it out so it can pay the civil service, this was the minister's reply:
X presume in due course when I announce it to the house.
I asked a supplementary question which reads:
As a supplementary question, may I ask the Minister of Finance what he intends to use for money when his present supply runs out.
The reply of the minister was this:
I am afraid that I could not answer that question because the occasion has not arisen yet.
Interim Supply
Despite that effort to bring to the attention of the government the fact that something should be done, and done then, about supply, nothing was done by the government, and so three days later, on Monday, May 28, I put another question to the Minister of Finance which can be found on page 4371 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Is the minister in a position yet to answer my question of Friday respecting when he is going to ask the house for interim supply so he will have some money in June? In the meantime, can he assure civil servants that the present interim supply he has will make it possible for him to pay salaries on the 31st of May?
What was the answer of the Minister of Finance, speaking for this government that is now so concerned about civil servants? Here it is:
I am not in a position to answer the question, but I will make inquiries.
I thought that would bring forth an answer on the minister's initiative within a day or so, but it did not come. Accordingly, on May 30 I asked again. Here is my question as recorded on page 4461 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Finance. In view of the action that has been taken in the other place ostensibly to make it possible to get interim supply through in one day, can the minister now say when he intends to move for interim supply?
The minister's reply was this:
I cannot, Mr. Speaker, but as is customary I shall consult with the opposition groups before making the proposal.
There you have it, Mr. Chairman. Three attempts on my part during the month of May to bring to the attention of the government the fact that something needed to be done to get interim supply so civil servants could be paid. But what was the government concerned about then? It had only one preoccupation, namely, getting its precious pipe line bill through the house. On Friday when the Prime Minister made his appeal to the house he said something to this effect, that it was usual at this stage to ask for interim supply. I have not turned up the exact quotation but I know that the words "at this stage" are there. May I remind the Prime Minister and the government that one has to stretch words a bit on June 8, or today on June 11, to say that this is the stage at which interim supply is usually sought for the month of June. I have taken the trouble to check back through the Hansards for the past 16 years-those happen to be the Hansards that I have in my office-covering the last four parliaments of which I have been a member. I checked every interim supply bill during those 16 years, and I shall say something in a moment about the picture

Interim Supply
as a whole, but first I want to say something about supply for the month of June.
After all, that is what is before the house now, supply for the month of June. I tell you, Mr. Chairman, from my research, that not in a single June during the past 16 years-you may go back further, but that is as far as I went in my research-not in a single instance has supply for June not been obtained prior to the end of May. Indeed in some cases it was obtained several days or even weeks before the end of May. Not once in the last 16 years, through all the war years and all the post-war years and all the troubles and fights that we have had in parliament, not once has the government laid aside its request for interim supply for the month of June because there was some other issue that was more important. It was only the pipe line that became more important than interim supply in this instance.
Let me put these dates on record. In 1940 it was obtained on May 28; in 1941, on May 29; in 1942, on May 26. In 1943, the motion which led to obtaining supply was actually made on May 11. There was a bit of debate and even with the debate that took place it was obtained in this house on May 17. In 1944 it was obtained on May 26. The year 1945 was an election year and supply for the months of May, June, July and August was obtained on April 13. In 1946 it was asked for on May 6 and obtained on May 26; in 1947 it was obtained on May 13. In 1948 it was again obtained on May 13. The year 1949 was also an election year and on April 30 a sufficient supply was put through for June, July, August and September. In 1950 it was obtained on May 30. In 1951 it was obtained on May 30. In 1952 it was obtained on May 29. In 1953 the final supply bill was put through on May 14. That, of course, was again an election year. In 1954 it was obtained on May 27 and in 1955 it was obtained on May 26.
There is the record of 16 years, Mr. Chairman; never later than May 30. Even apart from the instances of the election years it was obtained in some instances as early as May 13 and asked for in one year as early as May 6. In other words, the government knows from its past practice that the time to ask for interim supply for the month of June is in the month of May before its May money runs out.
I will tell the present Minister of Finance that he is personally aware of how these things should be handled. Indeed, last year in June when he was seeking interim supply for the month of July I asked him if the fact that he was seeking only one month's

supply meant that he hoped the main estimates would be through before the end of July. This was his reply as found at page 5274 of Hansard for June 24, 1955:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
There is no certainty at the moment, Mr. Chairman, that that will be so.
Then I ask that these words be noted:
If we are here on the 25th or 26th of July, I shall make another motion similar to this.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, despite the minister's innocence in his reply to my questions in May of this year, from his statement of last June it is clear that he knows that the time to ask for interim supply is before the end of the month in which the government's current interim supply runs out. This year the government would not do that even when we asked them to. They would not even consider the matter; no, it had to wait until the precious pipe line bill was through and then we are asked to bail the government out of the situation in which it finds itself.
With regard to the instances in the past, I might also point out that in addition to all these cases where supply for the month of June was obtained in the previous month, in the whole period of 16 years the only occasion I can find where interim supply for any month was obtained after the first of the month was in the fall of 1945. That, as hon. members will recall, was an election year. In fact, the 1945 election was held 11 years ago today. As the result of arrangements made previous to the calling of that election, interim supply ran out on August 31. The new parliament did not meet until September 6. What did Mr. King do? He took the matter up in the house the very first day, let the house understand that the treasury was empty and that interim supply would be needed. He indicated he had spoken to leaders of the groups opposite and arrangements were made for an interim supply bill to be put through on the 11th of September. That is the only instance across the 16 years where there was any delay in interim supply to a date beyond the first day of the month for which supply was to be voted. That of course was for a very justifiable reason; namely, there had been an appeal to the country and a general election.
I might also tell the house that in 1942 when supply was sought on May 26 by Mr. Ilsley a rather interesting situation developed. I am sure the Prime Minister will remember it because he was then a new member of the house and that was his first session. He was present that day because he answered a question that was put to him on the orders of the day. He was minister of justice at the time. It so happened that

Mr. Ilsley on that occasion asked for two months' supply. The house was in an angry mood over some things that had happened although it had much less cause to be angry than might be the case at the present time. As the result of a considerable debate Mr. Ilsley had to agree on the floor of the house to cutting his interim supply bill in half. It was only the 26th of May but he said to the house, "We need this money now; we need it to pay bills". He was talking about the month of June. The then leader of the opposition, Mr. Hanson, suggested the two months' supply be reduced to one and called upon the the minister of finance to accept the reduction to half of what he was asking the house to give him. Mr. Ilsley replied that he had no option, but that he had to accept. He recognized that the gift of supply was in the hands of the House of Commons.
This government, concerned as it has been to get its pipe line through, has paid no attention to the proprieties concerned with obtaining interim supply from the house and has let all its established practices go by the board. Now it comes before parliament and expects us, despite its failure to respond to the concern we demonstrated in May for the civil service, to bail the government out. I say, Mr. Chairman, the issue is not the salaries of our civil servants. Our position on that is clear. Like the Leader of the Opposition, we feel that although others may have been victimized by the government's action the civil service should not also be the victim of what this government has done. In our view it is a moral issue. What we now have is an executive which has treated parliament in a despotic manner, coming before parliament and asking it for the tools to carry on in the normal way just as if nothing had happened. It comes before parliament as if it had moral authority. We claim that it does not. In our view the honourable course for the government is to withdraw this request and come before us with an assurance that there will be a dissolution, whereupon we would grant whatever supply is necessary. If the government is not prepared to deal with it in that way we can only assume this government is not one that can be appealed to on the moral grounds which we feel are basic to this whole situation.
Mr. Chairman, it is not possible for a free parliament to have done to it what we have suffered here in the last few weeks and then for it to go on in the normal way. In our view the civil service and others should not be made to suffer, but in our view the government has no moral authority to make the request that it now lays before this house.
Interim Supply

Mr. Chairman, the ideal situation would be, of course, to have the estimates through the committee before the end of the financial year; then it would not be necessary for the government to ask for interim supply at any time; but we know from experience and past history that that has been impossible. Consequently it is necessary for the government some time before the end of the session to ask for interim supply as it is doing today.
Now, I have listened very carefully to the arguments that have been advanced today. I have thought back over the years when I have heard similar arguments advanced on many another proposition put forward by the government. At one stage I want to ask the hon. gentleman who was speaking if the situation with respect to the government's request for interim supply was any different fundamentally from the situation which exists when the government is asking for support for any proposition it puts forward. The opposition has argued on every occasion, I think, that I have ever heard in the house when the government has put forward a proposition, that the government ought not to do it because it did not enjoy the confidence of the people of the country. It does not matter what the proposition is, that is the position taken by the opposition; and the only difference it seems to me at the present time is that feelings are a little more in evidence than they were on previous occasions. There is perhaps more evidence of anger than there has been at other times.
I suppose if one were to take seriously the argument advanced here today about this being a dishonourable thing, one would have to consider the reverse position and argue that when we agree to an estimate passing we are indicating our belief in the normal integrity and the support by the country necessary for those who administer it. That is just about the last argument that could be advanced. It is just as reasonable to suppose that one argument could apply as that the other could apply.
I do not look upon this as a dishonourable request at all, and I suppose the reason I do not is that I do not think the government acted in a despotic manner in getting the pipe line bill through. Therefore I am not carrying around a lot of anger and bitterness in my soul because of what happened. I must say that I feel very bad about what happened, but that feeling has not been engendered by any belief I have that the government acted in a despotic manner.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has indicated his concern for the civil service. I have tried to put myself in

Interim Supply
the position of the Minister of Finance on any one of the last days of May when the request for information was made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I am wondering what the Minister of Finance thought as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre expressed concern or simulated concern for the civil service. I know I would have thought to myself that that was clever of the hon. member in trying to have something else brought before the house so that the bill being considered at that time would carry over June 7. I am not going to say that that was what was in the hon. member's mind, but believe me that is the thought I would have had if I had been in the position of the Minister of Finance at that time.
I wonder if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre or the Leader of the Opposition would give a clear undertaking today that if the Minister of Finance had called a recess for one day, let us say on May 29, 30 or 31, to ask for interim supply, they would have taken the normal time to discuss it and then got back to the pipe line bill. If they would give that unequivocal undertaking, then that would be an answer that they would have supported it without using it as the means to hold up government plans. If that were the case, then I would be ready to change my attitude, but under the circumstances I can only believe that they would have seized on that interim supply to hold things up beyond the date that was named as the terminal date beyond which they could not go with that bill.
It has been said that the government should have asked for interim supply at an early date. I think they should have done that as it would have been better for everybody, but I have tried also to think when they could have asked for it within the past three or four weeks with any chance in the world of getting it. I am of the opinion that they have asked for this interim supply at the earliest possible time available to them.
An effort has been made to stress that the government is a dishonourable government, that the government is a despotic government, and for that reason we ought to hold up interim supply. I am not claiming any virtue at all in that regard; I simply say that as the government has bills to pay, as time in running out and as we are going to have plenty of time to discuss the estimates in the regular manner and to do the business of the house in the regular manner, it would seem to be the best thing for members of this House of Commons representing the people of this country to get interim supply through and go on with the business of the house.

I would certainly suggest to the Minister of Finance that he bring the main departmental estimates before us as soon as possible so that we may have ample opportunity to go into them and have all the discussion required in the interests of good government in this country.

Mr. Chairman, before we vote on this question I should like to ask the Prime Minister one or two questions. It seems that the government has once more placed a deadline before the house. It seems to be the rule rather than the exception to have government by deadline. I for one resent that. If the government is going to operate in that way this bill should have been introduced by the Minister of National Defence, who is the only one with enough artillery to carry it through.
It seems to me that this is the proper time for the government to disclose some of its plans with regard to legislation. The government has been in such a great hurry to give away the taxpayers' money to United States capitalists that in my opinion they have completely ignored the Canadian people. We are wondering whether the government has any plans for legislation to better the lot of old age pensioners. We want to know what the government is going to do about blind pensioners. We also want to know when the government is going to straighten out the regulations under the Disabled Persons Act. These are things that may not appear to be huge things percentagewise as compared with the $103 million pipe-line bill, but they are important to many thousands of Canadians.
I must remind the government that it is several years since those who are recipients of old age pensions had an increase in their pensions. Since that time there have been two increases in civil service salaries, two increases in judges' salaries and at least one increase in the pay of the armed services. With the cost of living rising all over the country, people are asking when old age and blind pensioners are going to receive some consideration. This session is nearing its end and so far there has been no indication from the government as to whether they intend to introduce legislation this session with regard to old age pensions, blind pensions and the regulations under the Disabled Persons Act. I think this committee deserves answers to those questions before we vote on this motion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I just want to deal with one thing that was raised, the question that was asked as to what the opposition would have done if there had been time set aside when this motion could have been dealt with. I would point out that

after the pipe-line bill was introduced other business was dealt with on Wednesday, May 16. It would have been possible at that time for the government to have asked for interim supply, as it should have done well in advance of May 31. I point that out so the intervention by the hon. member for Peace River will not leave the impression that there was no opportunity for this to be done.
I do not wish to extend my remarks beyond saying that this is June 11 and the interim supply we are now dealing with runs from the beginning to the end of June only. I trust that when we are next called upon to deal with this matter it will be done in plenty of time. Of course the attitude we adopt at that time will depend entirely upon the circumstances of the case.

Mr. Chairman, I am not at all surprised that the government do not want to go to the country, as I have no doubt they have been reading the editorials which have been published during the past few weeks in newspapers across Canada. From editorials in regard to the pipe-line legislation itself, there were newspapers that supported it and newspapers that opposed it, but in regard to what this government did to the rules of this house the newspapers of this country have been almost unanimous. What we should ask from this government before we grant interim supply is: is this government from now on going to run this parliament according to the rules of this parliament? That is the question that should be asked.
I am rather surprised how easily my friends on my left have been bought. They used to associate the C.C.F. with the Liberal party and the Liberal government. We were socialists in a hurry; the Liberals were socialists who were not in quite such a hurry. But the socialists that were not in quite such a hurry have become quite acceptable socialists just because they helped to buy a little gas that the province of Alberta has to sell. Surely the support of no party was ever bought so cheaply.
As I have said, that is the assurance that the Leader of the Opposition should ask- and he is in a much better position to ask it than we are-from the government, while they are taking time to rehabilitate themselves and hoping that the public will forget what they have done to parliament and that, when the next election comes around some time in 1957, the odor in which they stand with the public will not be quite as bad as it is today.

Perhaps I do not understand all these words of diplomacy but am I to understand, from what the Prime Minister said at the presentation of this resolution, that at the present time the government is asking, because of the situation in which they are in, that all they require now is the one-twelfth of the estimates and that, if that is passed-and of course it must be passed, because the bills have to be paid-that means that the house is not going to adjourn this month or next month, either for a meeting in the fall or for the purpose of an election; but, if they get the one-twelfth of the money they require to pay their bills for the month of June, this house carries on with all normal business until it is finished, and that includes discussion of all estimates; and, if they are not finished by the end of June, then they come back again for interim supply? There has not yet been a straightforward statement as to the intention of the government. I guess that is the intention, but I think all of us would like the Prime Minister to get to his feet now and say point-blank what is the situation with all business of this house, all supply and all estimates?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

The situation at this time is that we are asking for one month's supply and that we intend, when that supply is granted, to proceed with the business of the house in the ordinary way. We do not expect that the estimates will be passed by the end of June, and we do expect that at that time it will be necessary to ask for further interim supply, and we intend to carry on with the business of the house in the normal way. Now I cannot go beyond that. I cannot at this time make any commitments about things which cannot be foreseen and circumstances which might in the future arise.
The hon. gentleman knows that there are several hundred items in the estimates, and each one can be discussed. If each one were to be discussed, even if we were to sit here until Christmas, we would not get through

with the discussion ot each one of those estimates if we were not seriously intent upon disposing of the business of the house in the normal way.
I do not want to say anything at the present time that would appear to be controversial. There will be plenty of controversy about all these matters on appropriate occasions. But I would hope that, for the reasons that have been given-and I am not going to attempt to discuss at this time the qualifications that have been placed upon these reasons-the supply will be granted at this time and that we could then proceed in the ordinary way with the business of the house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, just before the question is put, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether there is any legislation that the government intends to introduce which is not yet before the house?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is' not, to my knowledge, any legislation that has not yet been indicated. There is the legislation with respect to the dominion-provincial fiscal arrangements, which is being completed and the tenor of which has been fully disclosed in the proposals that have been made to the provinces, and that have been tabled in the house and even printed as appendices to Hansard. The Minister of Finance did say that he had a succession duty bill that he expected to introduce but that he was not at all confident that there would be time to have it considered. Those are the only two outstanding things, except for one that was forecast by the Minister of Labour for some partial amendment of, I think, section 45 (2) of the Unemployment Insurance Act. I do not know of anything else that is not already before the house.

I am sorry to get up again, but I have to go by the words of the Prime Minister that the house will, if granted the one month's supply, carry on in the normal way. If it carries on in the normal way, we should then go through all the estimates, with all our rights of discussing all estimates. That cannot be done in this month of June.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

In addition, carrying on in the normal way includes all the business on the order paper, that is, bills and estimates and so on. If that happens and we carry on in the normal way-and that is the interpretation I would like-is that the interpretation of the Prime Minister of the normal way? At this session?

session.

Mr. Chairman, this is the annual resolution that precedes the introduction of the Canadian National Railways Financing and Guarantee Act. Hon. members will recall that in 1952 the form of this legislation was changed so as to include the financing of all capital expenditures whether authorized in that act or in earlier financing and guarantee acts. This procedure has been followed again this year.
The bill to be founded on this resolution is divided into three specific parts. The first part is to authorize the Canadian National Railways to incur capital expenditures up to $233,564,000. The second part authorizes the railway company to make capital expenditures prior to July 1, 1957, to discharge obligations incurred under this act which become due and payable after January 1, 1957 in the amount of $80 million. The third part authorizes the railway company to enter

Canadian National Railways into contracts for new equipment and for its general additions and betterments in the amount of $90 million. speechtext:
The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance has set out some of the salient facts with regard to this resolution. He is quite correct in saying that the committee on railways and shipping gave careful consideration to the budget presented by the president of the Canadian National. Mr. Chairman, I shall be only a minute. I was very fortunate to be on the sessional committee of railways and shipping and to have had an opportunity to question the president of the Canadian National Railways and to hear him explain the over-all financial picture. As a matter of fact, it is not something that I ever thought I would have a chance to do when I took my first ride at four or five years of age in my dad's caboose on the old Grand Trunk.
There still seems to be a very critical situation facing the Canadian National. Mr. Gordon outlined that at the present time all of these expenditures which we have and which are mentioned in the resolution are prudent expenditures, and the railway can be expected to make the necessary profit to take care of the fixed charges on the outlay which is provided in this resolution; but at the same time he has not avoided saying that the railway does face a critical period as the dieselization program is completed and the law of diminishing returns sets in. In connection with that program, at the present time the railway has been able to meet its fixed charges owing to the fact that there has been great savings in connection with the introduction of that new dieselization program. But if that saving does not continue, or if we do have a corresponding increase in wage costs and other operating expenses, then of course, he is going to face a very serious problem in the over-all financing of the road.
In this connection, the company faces a different proposition from that of its competitor, the Canadian Pacific Railway, because if that railway is unable to meet at a specific time the dividend that might be expected on some of its stock then, of course, the dividend is simply not declared; but under the recapitalization program of 1952 there is an indication that the Canadian National has been set up on a basis so that all of its fixed charges can be paid and, as a matter of fact, of necessity must be paid because the government continues as the guarantor of all of the obligations.
I am not an accountant, but it seems to me that sooner or later we shall have to remove some of the shackles which surround railway operations in Canada. Perhaps we should have a look at this thing in the reverse of the ordinary accounting methods. Since it is absolutely essential that the guaranteed indebtedness must be met we shall have to set aside an amount which is absolutely essential to the railway's continued successful

Canadian National Railways operation, an amount to meet the fixed indebtedness. We shall have to use that as a step in the formula and then arrive at a situation where the railway may look at its current operating position and examine its revenue as related to its expenses. If there is an indication that that amount cannot be met, then of course we shall have to give the railway an opportunity to earn the amount of revenue sufficient to meet its current operating expenses. Possibly that is the reverse of the way the operation is carried out at the present time. If operating expenses are so great that they do not allow a sufficient amount to be carried over against the fixed charges, then of course the government has to step in, as it has done in the past. Even taking the 1952 formula into account, it might have to step in and make payments to the people holding bonds. Mr. Gordon said this in the committee: these expenditures are prudent ones. As far as the capital outlay is concerned, they can earn their worth, if you want to put it that way. Then, taking a realistic approach, we must move back in our formula and ensure that the railway itself in its current operations is placed in a position where it can meet its current expenditures. As a matter of fact, if that were done it seems to me we would not be faced with the almost yearly problem of negotiation between labour and management which is very unsatisfactory because first of all labour does not feel that it is being allowed to bargain in an unfettered condition because of the over-all control that has been set down at the top, and management feels just as frustrated because it realizes that no matter what it does in connection with meeting the demands of labour it too is in a position where its over-all operation is pretty well surrounded by government regulation.
At each step it must come back here- perhaps not to this house, but certainly to an arm of the government-and say, "We are in this situation, are you going to help us out?" It seems to me it is about time we took a very realistic approach to the over-all financing problem which confronts the Canadian National Railways and gave considerably more leeway to management in its fight to stay ahead of the increasing operating costs. In so doing I think we would find we would have a much more satisfied labour group on the railway as well.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at each of the last six sessions of parliament bills have been introduced entitled the Canadian Forces Act, similar in purpose to the bill which will be introduced upon the adoption of this resolution. The bill to be introduced will be entitled the Canadian Forces Act, 1956, and will propose a number of amendments to statutes related to defence. This year the bill is more limited than has usually been the case, in that it contains proposed amendments to only two acts, the Defence Services Pension Act and the National Defence Act.
Three clauses of the bill contain amendments proposed to the Defence Service Pension Act. Two of these amendments are designed to facilitate administration of existing provisions in the Defence Service Pension Act and the other is designed to achieve uniformity in respect of pension payments to members of the three services who are pensioned as warrant officers or equivalent and are subsequently re-enrolled or accept appointments in the public service of Canada.
Nine clauses of the bill contain proposed amendments to the National Defence Act. The amendments to this act deal with a variety of subjects and embody in the code of service discipline some provisions contained in the new Criminal Code adopted at the last session of parliament. Others, it is hoped, will facilitate the administration of justice under the code of service discipline.


One proposed amendment would enable the commander of a unit to issue to persons accompanying his unit enforceable orders relating to the defence or evacuation of the unit area in the event of an enemy attack.
Another amendment proposed to the National Defence Act would incorporate in the code of service discipline provisions relating to persons driving Canadian forces vehicles while their ability to drive is impaired by alcohol or a drug.
An amendment is also proposed which would clarify the authority of the governor in council to make regulations in respect of the enforcement of discipline in service prisons and detention barracks.
A further proposed amendment would enable treasury board to authorize the payment of tolls in respect of the use by Canadian forces vehicles of facilities such as bridges, highways and canals where such tolls are payable by other users.
There are other proposed amendments to the National Defence Act designed to facilitate the administration of the code of service discipline and to effect other changes of a technical nature in the act.
Mr. Chairman, the foregoing amendments are directed to the efficient and equitable administration of our defence forces, and I therefore commend this resolution to the committee for its favourable consideration.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity of thanking the minister for his concise and illuminating description of the amendments which are to be proposed by the bill to follow this resolution. However, it seems to me that this is just another example of the government following a bad practice which is used as a precedent and then becomes routine.
For some years now we on this side of the house have pointed out how unsatisfactory it is to combine amendments to several acts in one bill. This year the Minister of National Defence even goes so far as to apologize for the fact that there are only two acts being amended in this 1956 version of the Canadian Forces Act. I cannot help feeling that as these acts have been in existence for a good many years it is not necessary to take up the time of the house year after year bringing in small amendments. Surely the main acts should be reviewed and brought up to date once and for all instead of having to bring in amendments year after year.
For instance, I am quite certain that there were bridges in existence last year, the year before and the year before that which exacted tolls from military vehicles. Why could not

this amendment have been brought in before? The Defence Services Pension Act has been in existence for some time. Surely it should have been discovered by this time that there was some difficulty about warrant officers being re-employed, re-enrolled or accepted in the public service of Canada. It does not seem to me that the time of this house should be taken up with such amendments. Next year the Minister of National Defence may be proposing another amendment to deal with sergeants or petty officers. Surely one big effort could be made to bring these acts up to date.
With regard to the amendments made necessary by the introduction last year of the new Criminal Code, I agree that these should be reflected in the military code of discipline. Therefore it is reasonable to expect that prompt action be taken and that the amendments be made. I sincerely hope that the code of military discipline has been carefully reviewed since the introduction of the new Criminal Code, and that it will not be necessary next year to bring in any further amendments.
I notice that there is to be an amendment to deal with the enforcement of discipline in service prisons and detention barracks. I do not suppose there is anything very new about that. Then we come to the amendment dealing with persons driving military vehicles while under the influence of liquor. Unfortunately there have been a great many instances of persons charged in the courts across the country with being under the influence while driving military vehicles. I think it would be a good thing to tighten up the discipline in respect to that, because it not only may cause grievous harm to innocent people who are in the path of such vehicles but it certainly brings the units concerned into very bad repute. On the information we have received, which is rather sketchy, I feel that we shall have to defer any further comments until we have the bill before us.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. I have a short statement on the bill which I shall read. Part III of the Livestock and Livestock Products Act deals with poultry production. Under its authority is operated a national breeding program for poultry, known as record of performance, and the hatchery approval policy. The latter policy involves provision for supervision of chick hatchery sanitation and operations. On request of the provinces this policy has been proclaimed for compulsory operation in all 

provinces but Ontario, Quebec and Newfoundland. It operates voluntarily in those three provinces.
There are two features of hatchery supervision which will be changed by the proposed amendments. At the present time, under the authority of section 43 (b) of the act it is required that all chicks sold from approved hatcheries be marked with a standard grade name. In the present stage of development of the poultry business these compulsory grades have little significance with respect to the economic value of the stock. It is proposed to discontinue the requirement for compulsory grading and to substitute for that a provision which will protect the use of such terms as "record of performance" when applied to poultry. That is the purpose of the amendment to section 43 (b).
The act at the present time requires by section 48 that all advertising by chick hatcheries be approved by the department before publication. Section 52 (g) at present makes it an offence to publish such advertising without approval. This approval of advertising is no longer considered necessary and it is proposed to repeal section 48 and paragraph (g) of section 52.
In various sections of the act reference is made to certain requirements with respect to chicks. For administrative purposes it is desired to apply those same requirements to hatching eggs, which is the purpose of the proposed addition of subsection 2 to section 42 of the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution proposes very briefly to extend the provisions of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act at the same rate and under the same regulations for the years 1957 and 1958. This Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act came into operation in 1948, and with certain changes in formula it has been assisting the gold mines since that date.
The emergency, so far as the gold mines were concerned, was due to rising costs of labour and materials and the fixed price for gold at $35 United States funds per ounce. During the war the gold mines had been restricted in obtaining certain materials, and consequently production was less than it could have been under normal circumstances. The payments under the act were to meet emergency conditions and to compensate, in some measure, for the restrictions that had been imposed.
The emergency, so far as rising costs and the fixed price for gold are concerned, still exists. There are many communities dependent solely on gold mining and it is proposed, therefore, to extend the period of time for another two years, 1957 and 1958, at the same rate that prevailed for 1955 and for this year, 1956.
Payments under the act have always been based on a formula which has two factors, namely the rate of assistance and the number of assistance ounces. The formula now in effect, and which this bill will extend for two years, is two-thirds of the amount by which the average cost of producing an ounce of gold exceeds $26-50 multiplied by two-thirds of the production in the designated year. The maximum assistance payment is $12-33 an ounce.
Applications for payment in any year are received up until June 30 of the following year. Advance payments are made on an 80 per cent basis, pending an audit of the gold mining company's books by the cost inspection and audit division of the Department of Finance. When the audit is completed the final payment of the 20 per cent holdback is approved. Under these conditions final payments are not yet complete for 1955 but payments are expected to be in the neighbourhood of $9,300,000.
11, 1956	4911
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
In 1954, under a formula which gave greater payments, the total cost when the final settlements are made is expected to be about $16,300,000. In 1953 payments amounted to $14,652,080.26. Payments have varied from a low of slightly under $9 million in 1950 to a high of more than $16 million in 1954. The rate of payment per ounce produced in 1954 was $4.22 and in 1953 it was $4.61, the highest rate ever paid.
Payments are made only to mines whose production of gold is 70 per cent of the total value of their output. In 1955 five lode mines suspended operations while one other mine was absorbed by the parent company. One new lode mine came into production in 1955 and one mine elected to sell on the free market and was ineligible for assistance. No mines were on the free market in 1954. Production of gold eligible for assistance payments under the conditions outlined were 3,795,248 ounces in 1954 and 3,301,501 ounces in 1955. No payments under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act are made for gold produced as a by-product recovered in the smelting of gold-bearing base metals. Thus, the gold that qualified for assistance in 1954 was 86-9 per cent of the total gold production, which amounted to 4,366,440 ounces, and in 1955 the corresponding figure was 72-4 per cent of the total gold production of 4,556,400 ounces.
The gold mines have made strenuous efforts to decrease their operating costs, and with marked success. They have done very well. There has been an increase in grade of the ore found in several mines, and on a recent trip up through the Red Lake camp I was pleased to note that many of the mines there have improved their position. One mine in the Northwest Territories has a very high-grade ore and is doing very well without gold mining assistance. In 1957 there may be as many as seven mines which, on account of the costs of production decreasing, will receive either no assistance or just a very small amount under the terms of the act. Other mines, however, are in a life and death struggle for existence, and some may have to close in the next two years.
It has been estimated by officers of my department that if assistance payments were discontinued at the end of 1956, when the present act expires, 18 or 20 mines with an annual production of about 700,000 ounces of gold would quite likely close after a two or three years' salvage period. During the salvage period the gold now in sight would be mined but no new ore would be sought by further exploration. These mines when closed would be permanently lost.
4912	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
For the past several years there has been very little prospecting for or development of new gold mines, and the number of gold producers dropped in 1955 to fewer than half the number producing in 1941, the peak year of production. Most of the potential gold mines which are in the development stage are located in or near proven gold camps, and there appears to be little interest to move beyond those localities. Many of the gold mines, in fact, have used money received from gold production to go into other mining ventures. I think we are all familiar with the names of the mines. Gold mines have branched out into other fields such as iron, oil and uranium development.
I could name several mines but I do not think it would be wise for me in my capacity as Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to name any mines specifically. I do say this, that the companies that are engaged in gold mining are really mining companies and in many instances they have plowed their profits back into further exploration and new development of base metals as well as gold.
It will be apparent that the continuation of the emergency gold mining assistance has aided many of the gold mines to remain in operation so the communities dependent on them have continued to maintain a reasonable standard of living. It has provided money for new mining developments, as I have said, and they have contributed in this way to the general prosperity which mining is now enjoying, and which has been reflected in the economy of Canada.
The contribution of the gold mines to the Canadian economy can be summarized in a few sentences. The amount of new wealth produced in gold in 1955 was valued at $157,305,152. Salaries and wages paid in 1954 were $63,578,156; fuel and electric power purchased amounted to $6,987,528; plant and equipment installed amounted to $6,385,260, and other supplies purchased amounted to $38,814,500. It is estimated that the total number of employees in 1954 was almost 18,500.
Since the inception of the gold mining assistance in 1948 the amount paid out to March 31, 1956, is over $90 million. This applied to 26 million ounces, or an average of $3.48 an ounce. It is calculated that payments in 1955 will probably reach $9,300,000.
It is expected that if production costs remain the same for 1957 as for 1955 the cost of assistance in 1957 will be approximately $8,600,000. This decrease from the present estimate of $9,300,000 in 1955 and $8,900,000 in 1956, even though it is at the same rate as provided at the present time, is due to the
[Mr. Prudham.l
fact that several mines are now mining better grade ores and therefore will receive less help and, as I said before, a few will probably go out of existence.
There has been a marked improvement in efficiency in the last few years and for this the management and the men deserve a great deal of credit. Increased costs for the coming year, of course, would tend to increase payments under the act, but I predict that the present trend toward lower payments under the act will continue.
Gold mines are continuing to make, as I said before, a very valuable contribution to the over-all economy of Canada, and we think the further aid for the years 1957 and 1958 is entirely justified.

The minister has told us the emergency arose during the war when the price of gold was fixed at a certain price and when the costs of labour were increasing. Well, the price of gold is still fixed and labour is still going up and up and is much higher than it was at the time the bill was originally introduced. Possibly some consideration could be given to changing the name of the act.
I am reminded of the wartime income tax act which was introduced in 1917 as a temporary measure during the first war and was continued under the same name until about three years ago, when we finally dropped the word "wartime" out of the title and put it on the straight basis of the Income Tax Act. It may be that if this act is to be carried on it should not be called an emergency act but that some consideration should be given to changing the title to put it on the other basis.
Certainly the contribution which has been made by the industry, as the minister said,

One is faced with the possibility which the minister suggests of a substantial number of mines perhaps closing during the year. It presents a problem to the minister in the administration of this particular industry which I think is something that has to be dealt with on more than an emergency basis or from instalment to instalment as the minister proposes to do just now. I realize, too, of course, there are other mining industries as well as gold mining which are facing trouble and disaster, and there is one on which some of us could talk more competently than on this. As I said, I certainly am not trying to discuss the merits of this at all. I simply say that when the bill on which this resolution is based comes before us for second reading we will then have an opportunity to debate its merits and the application of the general principle as such, and I shall reserve any further comments for that debate.

If you wanted to have a little vegetable garden you would have to drag in the earth. Just north of that we have what is called the small clay belt. It has some of the finest soil you can find in any country in the world. The people there grow wonderful vegetables, but not in large enough quantities to justify the establishment of the costly storage facilities you would have to have if you were going to hold over your root vegetables in order to export them when you could get a good price. This clay farming area depends on the mining municipalities nearby for its markets. North of that clay belt we have the Kirk-land-Larder mining area which is almost solid rock with no soil at all. North of that again, and running into the riding of my colleague the hon. member for Timmins, we have a sand belt, and then a rocky belt and then the great clay belt. This part of Ontario will one day be one of the finest parts of Canada, and not only just for mining. I am happy to support this resolution preceding the bill. The minister has explained that all the proposed bill seeks to do is extend the emergency gold mining assistance payments for another two years, namely 1957 and 1958. By making this federal cost-aid policy apply over the next two years instead of only one, it will now be possible for the management of Canadian gold mines to plan their future operations with greater assurance. The two-year extension will serve to strengthen the stability of this industry in Canada.
When this legislation was first introduced in this house eight years ago, we all knew it was not meant to be a cure-all for the troubles that beset this important mining industry. Rather it was planned as emergency help over what was hoped to be a comparatively limited period of years. The industry had been caught in a progressive squeeze between rising production costs on the one hand and a fixed price for its product on the other. That condition still applies, and I assume that some form of federal assistance will be continued to gold mines as long as the industry remains caught in an unfair and ruinous situation.
By this renewed measure of federal aid the government acknowledges that the gold mining industry of Canada is worth preserving and encouraging. It is the pioneer industry of the north country and has done more than any other activity to push back our frontiers of settlement and give Canada depth as well as width. It is an industry that provides employment as well as a market for machinery and supplies. Gold mining is and has been the mainspring of our entire mining economy, especially in the north. The search for gold spurs the search for other minerals.
In 1953, the last designated year under the legislation for which complete figures are available, 20 gold mines in the Yukon territory received a total federal subsidy amounting to $536,954.67. I find that applications for assistance for the designated year 1954 will continue to be received in Ottawa up until June of this year.
There is one strange inherent contradiction in federal gold mining policy in its application to the Yukon to which I wish to draw special attention at this time, which is causing gold mining operators in the Yukon considerable anxiety. Placer gold mining companies in the Yukon receive federal costaid assistance, as indeed they should. I fully support this form of encouragement and only wish the amount could be increased. On the other hand, the federal government discourages this placer mining industry by fastening
11. 1956	4921
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act upon it a heavy special tax that has all the earmarks of rank discrimination. I refer to the gold export tax. In its severity and unfairness, as well as its evident contradiction of the purpose of emergency gold mining assistance, this tax provision appears to represent the height of absurdity.
In 1953, for example, one placer gold mining company in the Klondike district paid $20,217 on all gold shipped out of the Yukon, whatever its disposition. This represented over 78 per cent of the year's profit on the company's operations. That imposition is bad enough, but the discriminating feature enters when we realize that the equivalent tax or royalty under the provisions of section 95 of the Yukon Quartz Mining Act would have amounted to $476. For 1954 the equivalent figures are $25,179 export tax on placer gold in contrast to $5,535 on quartz gold under the Yukon Quartz Mining Act.
My contention is that the gold export tax should be reduced in line with the rates of royalty under the provisions of section 95 of the Yukon Quartz Mining Act. The question involves two principles. First of all, is it fair and sound that a depressed industry should be obliged to pay such an exorbitant tax? And secondly, if the royalty is fair and sound in principle, is the amount of the royalty reasonable? I say not.
The gold export tax may have had some justification when it was established in 1897, inasmuch as gold was being shipped from the Yukon to the United States and our government felt Canada should secure some revenue from the tremendous production of gold at that time. Today the situation is much different.
I do not say that this export tax should be entirely abolished. When it was first imposed, gold was being exported from the Yukon to the United States and it was felt that the people of Canada should derive some financial benefit from the depletion of the mineral resources of this country. But let me again reiterate that the present rate of this so-called gold export tax is a heavy and unfair burden on placer mining operations and should be sharply reduced, at least to the point where it is at the same level as taxation on the product of gold quartz mining activity.
This appeal has the support of three major business organizations of this country. I refer to the British Columbia and Yukon chamber of mines and its branches, the Vancouver board of trade and the Yukon territorial council, which on March 28 of this year passed the following resolution:
Whereas an export tax on gold mined in the Yukon territory was imposed in 1897 to provide revenue from shipments to the United States;
4922	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act
And whereas practically all gold mined in the Yukon today is shipped to the Royal Canadian Mint at Ottawa;
And whereas it is a discriminating tax levied solely on gold shipped from the Yukon;
And whereas it increases the burden of an industry struggling to survive due to ever increasing costs and the fixed price of gold;
Therefore be it resolved that this council recommend that an adjustment be made of the export tax on gold mined in the Yukon Territory.
By bringing the placer gold export tax into line with the tax levied on quartz gold, the government would be encouraging an industry which provides important employment in one of Canada's most northerly communities. Gold mining costs in the Yukon are already high enough. The labour costs of one producer is 70 per cent of the total cost of production. If this export tax is permitted to continue at its present rate serious curtailment of operations may occur.
This export tax on Yukon placer gold, which yields over $40,000 a year in revenue to the federal treasury, has the effect of adding approximately 37 J cents in additional production cost to every ounce of gold produced. There has been no change in this gold export tax provision since 1902. It will not require a change in the legislation, merely a change in the regulations. An amendment to the act itself would be necessary only if the tax were eliminated altogether.
I appeal to the government on behalf of all placer gold mining companies in the Yukon to drastically reduce the rate of the so-called gold export tax to provide encouragement for this depressed mining industry.
