I shall not get into an argument on that because I am not very well informed apart from the terms of the act. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked what we were doing in a constructive way to provide alternate employment for people in the gold mining industry. I would remind him that the geological survey of Canada has about 75 parties in the field this year. Every year they are mapping the geology of Canada and the records, maps and statistics which they have compiled form the basis for a great many mineral discoveries.
I could mention a few recent discoveries which were based on the reports, maps and statistics compiled by the geological survey, in many cases years ago. One outstanding example is the great iron ore development in Labrador which was based on geological reports made before the turn of the century. More recent ones are the Manitouwadge ore discovery and the discoveries at Blind River, and to a large extent the discovery in New Brunswick.
I submit that this is the most constructive effort that could be made to keep the mining industry advancing and to provide alternate employment for people engaged in a particular line of endeavour which seems to be facing difficult times. I know of one gold mine in Quebec which is nearing the end of its life. During this last year they discovered a copper deposit within 20 miles, which they are now developing. They will use their gold mill for the processing of that copper ore and the community will be assured of continuation. I know of another area in Manitoba which has been depending on gold exclusively for a number of years. The last report I have is that the mill will be turned over to the processing of nickel ore.
I do not think we should take a short-term view of this. It is true that mines come and go, but in the over-all picture a really constructive effort is being made by the industry itself, by the federal government and by the provincial governments to develop these great mineral resources. I am confident that

the gold mining industry through its own efforts and through the development of base metals and other minerals in the same areas and in other parts of Canada will come through this emergency period and will soon be self-sustaining. I think it would be a negative approach indeed to take the money which we are now advancing to the gold mining industry and use it to move people away from that industry.
Our economy in Canada is very interdependent. The mining industry is a large consumer of agricultural products and as I mentioned this afternoon of the products of our forests and factories. When one makes a trip to these areas he cannot help but be impressed by the large consumption of goods that is taking place.
I think that is all I have to say at the moment unless some hon. member has another point to bring up.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say just a few words in support of what the hon. member for Timiskaming has said. I think everyone who has commented on what she had to say missed completely the point she was making. I am in sympathy with her because I represent exactly the same kind of area. During the present session a motion was moved in the house and we had a broad and comprehensive discussion of the whole question of ghost towns investments and areas which were working on wasting resources. There is no need to repeat what was said then.
The Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act justifies itself on the grounds that it creates employment and keeps up industry. On that basis I support it. As the minister has indicated the amount of assistance has dropped from $16 million to $9 million, which indicates that many of the mines are going into the free market. The mines to which this assistance is applicable are marginal mines. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam does not understand that if this gold mining assistance act was not applicable to those particular mines they would close. There would be no employment and the benefit that the miner gets out of this assistance is that he has a job and there are some wages paid. Otherwise he would not have a job.
The point I wish to make is this. The hon. member for Timiskaming has pointed out that all mining areas are the same. They go up, they reach their peak, and they peter out. In the meantime there are millions of dollars invested in the community, in schools, sewers, streets and everything that goes to make up a community. If the community is
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act allowed to go down with the industry, then that total investment on the part of the people is lost.
What was suggested earlier in the session was that realizing that mining is a wasting resource, that it will reach its peak and go down, there should be a continuing research committee set up by both provincial and federal governments to study the area and find out what kind of subsidiary industry might replace the mining industry when it goes out, so the investment on the part of the people in the community may not be lost.
This is a young country and it is growing, and there is much room for development. Over the next 50 years there will be many people in all sections of it. I am sure that, either in northern Ontario or in the mining areas of Cape Breton or in Nova Scotia or British Columbia, if a proper body were set up to make a proper analysis of the future so the investment in a community may not be lost, subsidiary industry in those areas could be found that would be useful in the future. That was the angle the hon. member took, and I support it very strongly.
I take exactly the same view. The coal mines are going down. The miners are moving out to British Columbia. Many of them are going out to the logging industry. That is a long way from home. There are those -a few hundred-now going out to Steep Rock. These people have homes and investments in a community. Many of them are leaving families. They do not want to uproot themselves. I am sure that if a proper study were made of the areas, suitable development could be found in these communities to retain the investments that have been made over many years.
Coal is subsidized, and rightly so, because it provides a means of livelihood. It is holding up communities that otherwise would go out overnight. On that ground this subsidy is justified. But I would stress again to the minister that subsidies are only a palliative, not a cure; that the crux of the whole problem is that sooner or later, whether or not you subsidize these mines, they are going to go out because they are a wasting resource. Ways and means should be found. At the present time research is more necessary than anything else the government could do to find ways and means of retaining the investment in these communities.
If we were an old country I would say it is a tough proposition, but we are not. The future is ahead of us. There is a terrific possibility of development in this country over the next 50 years, and in no section of it should there be any waste. Remember

Supply-Transport
that this is the last frontier. From every section of the world immigrants are coming into Canada, principally because there is no other place to go. We should not allow any sections of our community to become ghost towns or wastes or lost investments. We should be planning to rehabilitate these communities, and I think it can be done; but it requires a continuing research committee in order to do that. I am in hopes that the Gordon commission, when it makes its report, may have something to say on that particular point.
I do not want to deal with the point, because we beat this to death on a resolution during this session. I just wanted to say that the hon. member for Timiskaming was not asking for charity. She was justifying the measure before the house at the present time as a temporary measure, but what she was stressing was the investment in the community and the fact that sooner or later it was going down anyway and that efforts should be made on the part of the government to provide subsidiary industries to protect the investment the people have in these communities.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Prudham thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 417, to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
On this particular item of the estimates there are a great many things that many hon. members would like to say, but I am going to confine my remarks to a subject (Mr. Gillis.l
which has been of great interest to me and, I believe, to some other hon. members of this house. That is the subject of search and rescue organizations on the great lakes.
First of all, though, I should like to make some brief remarks regarding airport facilities, particularly at Malton airport, Toronto. The subject of airport facilities has been under considerable discussion in the past. I know there have been great plans to improve those facilities. The other day I saw some very fine pictures of what the Ottawa airport is to be like. I was very glad to see that. People coming to Ottawa on business and the public generally are very glad to see that improvements are to be made. However, Malton airport is, I suppose, almost the busiest, if not the busiest airport in Canada, and the facilities there for the travelling public are deplorable.
There is one little scheme they have there which is of interest. You pay 10 cents to stand on the roof and watch the aircraft coming and going. It is rather comfortable, except that there are only one or two benches on which one may sit after paying the 10 cents. In the waiting room below, where most people wait for planes as they come and go, or are delayed, as is frequently the case, there is not enough accommodation for people to sit down. There are ladies, some with children, old people, cripples and so on, and usually the crowds hanging around Malton airport are much like the crowds we have seen in the galleries of the house and in the corridors of the building in the last couple of weeks.
I hope the minister will tell us that plans are going to be made to improve the seating capacity of the waiting rooms at Malton airport. I know they are building something outside, sort of a shed or canopy to keep the rain off people going out to the planes, but there certainly is not enough accommodation. The only thing that Malton airport normally resembles at practically any time of the day when planes are arriving and departing is, with all respect, a twentieth century black hole of Calcutta.
To get back to the remarks I had originally intended to make, they have to do with the matter of a great lakes search and rescue organization to which I have referred already during this session. However, I should like to make some additional remarks. Now that the drowning and accident season on the great lakes is again upon us, this matter has come very much to public attention. There have been numerous editorials in virtually all the newspapers in the southern part of Ontario which, of course, is that part of the country most affected.

I am not going to refer to the remarks I have made in the house on other occasions during this session and last session with respect to the need of a coastguard service on the great lakes. I do not intend to do so because anybody who is interested can always refer to those remarks. But I should like to bring forward some additional information at this time. The whole subject of an improved search and rescue organization on the great lakes has become very much in the public mind and is becoming increasingly so. To summarize what I have pointed out on other occasions, this is largely due to the great increase in population in southern Ontario, the increase in the material wealth of the people since the war, more leisure time and the fact that people have taken to boating to a great extent.
To show the interest that has arisen this spring in this regard I should like to refer briefly to certain editorials. I do not intend to read them in their entirety but I wish to refer them to the minister. First of all there was an editorial in the Tillsonburg News of April 5, 1956, which is one of the largest weekly papers in Ontario. The editorial is headed, "Protection Needed on the Lakes," and ends with these words:
The federal government, in whose jurisdiction the great lakes fall, should give the matter consideration. Better protection is definitely needed.
I also refer to an editorial in the London Free Press of Thursday, March 29, 1956, headed, "Search and Rescue Service Necessary on the Lakes." It starts off with these words:
With the summer boating and swimming season approaching, Wallace Nesbitt, M.P. for Oxford, has made a suggestion that merits the attention of the federal government.
Then it goes on to deal with the matter at some length and ends by saying:
This is a fault Ottawa could and should remedy. Mr. Nesbitt suggests that something like a coastguard service could be set up economically by employing university students on their summer vacations. It might be possible to integrate reserve naval personnel and boat club members in such a plan. In any case, the Oxford M.P. has introduced a suggestion too valuable to be cast aside.
Then I refer to an editorial in the Toronto Globe and Mail of Wednesday, May 9, 1956, headed "Why Not a Coastguard?" The Globe and Mail, I may say, has had editorials on this matter before. I believe this is the third editorial they have had. I shall not waste the time of the house reading this editorial. I should not say "waste the time of the house", but I shall not take the time of the house to read it because hon. members can always read it. However, it touches on the incident that occurred on lake Erie this spring
Supply-Transport
when a number of Canadian fishermen had their boats seized by the United States coastguard apparently for trespassing in United States waters. It points out that if we had some sort of coastguard service it could be used to warn Canadian fishermen to keep out of United States waters and warn them when they are getting into United States waters. Of course this would largely concern only lake Erie, because due to the lamprey problem and other things commercial fishing on the other great lakes is not so much concerned with this problem at the present time.
Then I also refer to another editorial that appeared in the Woodstock Sentinel-Review. This editorial is headed, "Boating Mishaps", and is of very recent date having been published on June 7, 1956, just a few days ago. It refers to the announcement made by Captain G. L. Johnston, assistant chief of the nautical division of the Department of Transport, concerning the future licensing of small boats on the great lakes, something which the minister referred to earlier this day. The editorial points out the great problem on the great lakes so far as search and rescue is concerned. It points out that there is no coordination among the services, and that many a life could have been saved had there been some sort of co-ordination.
I do not know what brought about this action on the part of the department. I hope that some of the remarks I have made in the past may have had some influence. However, I am quite sure that the Department of Transport and possibly even the minister have received letters from numerous organizations such as the lake Ontario search and rescue organization, which has been doing a particularly fine job in rendering service by helping people who have become lost and in trouble on the great lakes, and also has been doing very fine work in trying to publicize the situation and interest public opinion in this very important matter.
I do not know what caused these proposed changes, but in any event I am very glad to see that they are going to be made, and I certainly welcome the proposed amendments to the Canada Shipping Act. I do not wish to refer to that matter at this time because it will be discussed on another occasion in the house, but I see that under one of the proposed amendments to the act there will be regulation of the inland and minor waters of Canada and provision for the licensing of operators in such waters, and I am very glad that that is so. While this is not the whole loaf but only half a slice out of the whole proposed loaf, at least half a slice of bread is better than none at all.

Supply-Transport
Of course there is no doubt that when the Canada Shipping Act comes before us it will be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. At least I presume it will, and I should like to suggest to the minister now that he take under consideration the calling of witnesses before that committee when it is considering the bill. Since one of the amendments to the act is going to concern the regulation and licensing of boats on the great lakes, I should like to suggest to the minister that at that time the committee should call witnesses to give evidence with respect to all the information the committee may require, not only as to the proposed regulations but to provide the minister and the department with information as to the actual need for search, rescue and other similar services on the great lakes.
I see this suggestion was made indirectly by the hon. member for Northumberland in a speech he made earlier this year. I know I am not allowed to refer to remarks made in previous debates during the present session, but without quoting the hon. member directly I think I can say that he suggested that at the present time there was insufficient evidence before the Department of Transport to justify the setting up of a proper coastguard or search and rescue organization on the great lakes, and that we should hear witnesses.
Since the hon. member was, I presume, speaking on behalf of the government at that time-his speech certainly looked like it, to say the least-may I suggest that here is a chance for the government to call witnesses. They could call the president of the lake Ontario search and rescue organization. They could hear the presidents and other officials of the various boating and yacht clubs and also the provincial police and others. These people could appear before the committee while these amendments were being considered.
Then if the minister and the officials of the Department of Transport are not prepared to take my word for it, and are not prepared to take the word of some of the large, prominent newspapers in Ontario such as the Toronto Globe and Mail, the London Free Press and a large weekly like the Tillsonburg News, which are newspapers in the area directly concerned, I feel that, since the department had claimed through its spokesmen that there is insufficient evidence before it, when these amendments to the Canada Shipping Act are before the committee that will be the time to get this additional information.
As I have pointed out before in this house, there are certain rescue and search organizations such as the provincial police, the

R.C.M.P. and the R.C.A.F. air search and rescue organization at Trenton. These have all been referred to in the house and most hon. members are familiar with them. As I pointed out before, the big problem is coordination when an accident occurs. If a boat upsets and someone is in the water or a boat is lost in the fog on the great lakes, the question is with whom do you get in touch? Usually nobody knows; even the local officials very often do not seem to know. Eventually Trenton or someplace like that may be informed and under those circumstances will take steps to commence the rescue. Usually there is a heavy fog or a storm, and it is very difficult for aircraft to operate and try to locate boats lost in a fog.
The important element is time. If an accident happens and someone has to search for two or three hours to find out with whom to get in touch, very often the person involved is drowned. While they announce with great trumpeting that they have discovered the body, I do not think that is very much help to the family of the person concerned.
It has been suggested on other occasions by the hon. member for Northumberland that the present regulations are fine and that small boats have to have licences. That is true. It is my understanding that the purpose of licensing motors of 10 horsepower and above is to determine to whom they belong. I know the number has to be painted on the back in 3-inch letters, and if a boat overturns or is lost the authorities can determine to whom it belongs and can get in touch with relatives in case of a fatal accident. It has been pointed out that this is quite adequate, and that the R.C.M.P. are in charge of inspection services.
I should like to know, and perhaps if there is time the minister could tell us although I know it is not directly under his department, just how many R.C.M.P. constables there are in the province of Ontario who are running around inspecting small boats. I would be willing to warrant that there are not very many. I should like to find out if there are any R.C.M.P. constables inspecting small boats in Ontario, and just what they do. What kind of reports do they make? I would very much doubt that they make any report at all or have much activity in this regard. If they do, I would be most delighted to hear about it.
It has been already noted with some pleasure that there are amendments proposed to the Canada Shipping Act which will certainly be helpful in a small way in alleviating this problem. I should like to see further amendments to this act, and it might not be too late for the minister to consider amendments relating to safety devices in small boats.

These amendments might involve the provision of life jackets and the question of small children being obliged to wear such jackets when they are out on the great lakes. In addition, these boats might be fitted with flares or smoke signals of some sort.
Then the question would arise, who is going to enforce these regulations? This question occurs to me right away, even in relation to the proposed legislation. I note that clause 27 of the bill, paragraph (c), refers to the enforcement of any such order or regulation.

-but I was suggesting that there are certain things which are not included in these amendments. We have all had an opportunity of reading the proposed amendments, and I thought before they came before the house the minister should have an opportunity of considering whether or not he could make some further alterations to meet this problem. My remarks were merely directed to that end. However, I shall not continue with them, as I feel I have already said enough. I hope the minister will give the problem a little extra consideration.
There are just one or two other matters I would like to mention. In some previous remarks I made concerning this question I confined my suggestions to the minister, and to the government generally, to the point that the coastguard service on the great lakes be restricted to the summer months and largely to search and rescue work. I did not feel that a further expansion of the service into the customs and excise division to check contraband would be warranted at the present time. I felt the work should be largely limited to search and rescue work, but there might be one exception.
On lake Erie large commercial fishing activities are carried out and a very nasty incident arose there this spring, but apparently it was not too important. Some Canadian fishing tugs were seized by the
Supply-Transport
United States coastguard and taken to the city of Toledo, I believe it was, where fines were levied, and properly so. However, rumours do have a habit of spreading and there were a lot of newspaper reports about the incident which created a bad impression in the public mind. Incidents such as these do not encourage good feeling between ourselves and our great neighbour to the south, with whom we have always had the most friendly relationship.
If there were a Canadian patrol vessel on lake Erie it could warn our fishermen to keep out of those waters, and during the summer months it could also be called upon in case of boating accidents. I suppose that lake Erie has more small boats on it than possibly any other of the great lakes. I had some figures to show that in Ontario alone last year the number of registered small boats increased by 15,000. It is true, of course, that many of these would be in small inland waters which do not come under the federal transport department, such as the Muskoka lakes and so on, but a great number of them would be on the great lakes. The president of the lake Ontario search and rescue organization, which I suppose is the largest and most well organized of these volunteer organizations, has pointed out that there are 300,000 or 400,000 small boats of all kinds in Ontario, a very large proportion of which would be on the great lakes. This number would include canoes, rowboats, boats powered with motors under 10 horsepower and so on.
Since a great number of these boats are on lake Erie a patrol boat, in addition to giving information to Canadian commercial fishermen who work out of Port Dover and other ports, could perform this other very necessary work as well. Lake Erie is probably the most dangerous of the great lakes. It is very shallow and the slightest thunder squall will stir it up.
Since I mentioned this matter in remarks I made earlier I do not wish to duplicate them at this time. Therefore I shall bring my remarks on this subject to a close at this time, though I shall probably resume them, as the minister suggested, when the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act come up for consideration. However, I should like to close by referring to one news item. I started my remarks by saying that the accident and drowning season is upon us again. I should like to refer to a news item which appeared on Monday, June 4 last. It appeared in all the Ontario papers. I happen to have

Supply-Transport
a clipping from the Sentinel-Review Daily of Woodstock. The heading reads:
Missing Persons Safe After Ordeal On Lake
Three men and two women paddled their three outboard motorboats ashore today at nearby Whitby after drifting all night on lake Ontario.
The article goes on to give in some detail what happened. It says that fortunately the lake was calm. If it had not been calm there would have been a number of bereaved families. This item appeared early in the season. No doubt we shall have like articles appearing day after day during the remainder of the summer and the warm weather season until September. There will be headlines such as these in the paper saying that five people have drowned, two people have drowned, boat upsets, boat adrift for three days, persons missing, and so on. Every year it is the same.
As I said, the minister has apparently started to do something. Changes are to be made in the Canada Shipping Act, but I do not think they go far enough. I hope the minister and the officials of his department will consider doing something in this regard either by themselves or in co-operation with the appropriate authorities in the province of Ontario, because I do not think any of us want to see a repetition of what we have seen year after year, namely an increase in the number of drownings in the lakes in the summer time.

Mr. Chairman, it must be obvious to anyone who examines the estimates of the Department of Transport that one of the surprising things in the set-up of this government is the number of matters which should properly come under the Department of Transport but which are not actually there. One outstanding example, of course, is that of Trans-Canada Air Lines. It is a major transportation system in every way similar to the Canadian National Railways in so far as it operates as a transportation system, but we find that it does not report to the Minister of Transport.
In recent weeks in this house we have seen one of Canada's greatest advances or great beginnings in a new field of transportation, namely the trans-Canada transportation of gas. That has been pushed through the house, and whatever happens in that field will ultimately be reported to a minister other than the Minister of Transport. We find again that while the Minister of Transport has the responsibility for most canals, there are canals turning up under the aegis of the Minister of Public Works. We find that while the Minister of Transport has the responsibility for most wharves and most harbours, certain maritime
[Mr. Nesbitt.)
transportation operations carried on by the government respond again to the Minister of Public Works.
I was amused just before rising to discover that two of my colleagues who sit right next to me, one from the Kootenays and the other from Selkirk, are in this position. The hon. member for Kootenay West has an inland lake in his constituency, and the Department of Transport operates the aids to navigation, wharves, and the like. The hon. member for Selkirk, who sits immediately behind him, has an inland lake in his riding, namely lake Winnipeg, and apparently the responsibility for similar functions in his area come under the Minister of Public Works. Certainly that is so in so far as the wharves are concerned. I would suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that it is quite impossible to have any sort of efficient, coherent and sensible transportation operation in so far as the government is concerned when we have this widespread diversity of responsibility in various aspects of it.
It would seem that one of the first tasks which faces the Minister of Transport and his department is to go out and bring under the wing of his department in some sort of sensible pattern the operations carried on by the government which should properly be responsible to the Minister of Transport. One does not want to suggest why his department might have been burgled in the past and had these various operations either stolen from it or never given to it, but whatever the past reasons may have been the present situation is, from an administrative point of view, most unsatisfactory and could well be corrected.
That leads almost automatically to the suggestion of a national transportation policy of some kind for Canada. Here again we have the responsibility in various fields of transportation widely separated and governed by a number of different committees and groups, and this policy is causing inconsistencies and raising many problems which would not exist if we developed a more sensible and more coherent alignment of responsibility. I have as one authority at least no less than the Turgeon report of 1951 which, hon. members will recall, is the report of the royal commission on transportation. At page 280 of that report we find the commissioners pointing out, and I quote:
Today there are three separate bodies, each charged with the control (a more or less extensive control in each case) of a part of Canada's transportation system. They are the board of transport commissioners, the air transport board and the Canadian maritime commission. It must be difficult, with this dispersion of control, to apply to all of Canada's transportation agencies like principles of regulation for the accomplishment of a common purpose, viz. that of enabling

each agency to perform its service advantageously and properly as part of a national transportation structure. The tendency of a separate independent body is to formulate policy affecting transportation without regard to the relationship of the various agencies to each other. This anomaly should give way to the constitution of a central authority which will be able to take in hand the major task of co-ordinated control, having at its disposal all the benefit acquired from the experience of the separate bodies in recent years.
That is only one authority which could be quoted; there are many others, and they seem to agree along those fundamental lines. Of course, we realize that one of the principal factors in transportation today is highway transportation, and within the bounds of the provinces that is beyond dispute under the control of the province itself. By a finding of the privy council in England, if my memory serves me rightly, or a body of appeal in England at any rate, interprovincial highway transportation systems are essentially under the control of the federal government. Last year the federal government returned or abdicated that field-"abdicated" might be a better word-and decided to leave it to the provinces for the time being.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext: I think if you said it was under the control of the federal parliament it would be more exact.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
right, under the control of the federal parliament, if the minister prefers it, although since recent days we have seen great evidence that the federal parliament is being so completely subjugated to the government itself it might be said that any suggestion that matters are subject to the control of the federal parliament is rather a mockery, it seems to me.
The question of integrating highway transport by means of a national approach to transportation or a national transportation policy, as I have suggested, does present certain difficulties; however, we have managed in other fields, at times when the provinces had control of a given section or area of our economy, to work out a modus operandi by means of meeting with them, by means of discussion with them, which has brought about very satisfactory results in some cases.
It would seem to me something of that nature is urgently required in the present instance. Certainly it is unfortunate with the tremendous growth and development which is taking place in this country at the present time that we should have our manifold means of transportation-our airways, our railways, our maritime transportation, our highways, our pipe lines-all at sixes and sevens, the majority of them reporting to different bodies of control, the majority of
Supply-Transport
them quite properly competing with one another, but competing without any attempt at co-ordination on the part of the government which has none the less intruded itself by means of regulatory bodies into almost every one of the fields I have mentioned.
Nowhere is this intrusion more evident than in the field of railway transportation and nowhere, Mr. Chairman, is there greater need for a new and imaginative approach to the regulation of transport, the control of transport, than in the field of railway transportation. I do not think we can expect the free enterprise type of activity-which is represented by at least one of our great railroads in complete measure and a quasi-free enterprise type of activity by the other, the Canadian National Railways-I do not think we can expect them to operate indefinitely with success unless they have a genuine opportunity to express their managerial discretion and equal opportunity to act in accord with the basic principles of a free enterprise system.
There was a time when it was necessary to impose the strictest measure of control on railway transportation as such because at that time it occupied a monopoly position. When the railroads grew up, when they first laid their lines across this country, when they divided it almost into a checkerboard pattern with line after line, the only measure of competition was one railroad as against another railroad; there was no air transportation and in great parts of the country there was no opportunity for maritime transportation. There was no such thing as pipe lines, and the gasoline engine being almost unheard of in those days there was no such thing as highway transportation.
Therefore when you had a monopoly system of transportation as was the case with the railroads, it was perhaps necessary that a firm measure of control be exercised; but that measure of control, it seems to some of us, has been continued in almost the same pattern right down to the present despite the tremendous differences in the economic framework within which the railroads are now operating.
The highway transportation system in this country is today a major factor in the transportation and transit industry. Buses carry great loads of passengers; heavy transport trucks, each of which comes very close to carrying the same tonnage as a railway car, whine along the highways of this country day and night. Overhead, by the tens of thousands, passenger traffic is being taken away from the railroads by the airways. Overhead again, the high value freight and express traffic is being picked up by the airways. Under these

Supply-Transport
circumstances it seems to me the old pattern under which the railroads are held under rigorous control and given no opportunity to engage in ordinary economic enterprise which is available to most fields of enterprise in our economy is unrealistic in relation to the present day structure of our transportation pattern.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
Will the hon. member permit me to ask one question at this point? He has just spoken about the rigorous control of the railways, and a little earlier he spoke about the fact that what the railroads needed was the opportunity to exercise their managerial authority. The hon. member has gone on to describe the conditions which I take it he believed had changed the position of the railways from a monopoly to one in which they are now faced with vigorous competition.
I wonder if I might ask the hon. member what forms of rigorous control he has in mind that are now interfering with the operation of the railroads? I know it is very easy to talk in generalities, but I wonder if the hon. member would give one example of the type of control to which he is referring.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext: Perhaps I should have covered that point at the beginning, but I thought it would have been reasonably obvious and certainly it would have become obvious-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext: Well, if it is obvious let us have it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
However, I am very grateful to the minister for pointing out that I have not perhaps defined the particular field that was in my mind at the beginning of these remarks. I had particularly in mind the question of the rate structures of the railroads, and the necessity for the railroads at the present time to go through a complicated and lengthy process whenever they desire a lasting change in their rate structure; a process incidentally, Mr. Chairman, which very often has a tendency to result in rates which are unrealistic in the light of all the circumstances surrounding a particular situation.
Now, the minister does not need to take my word for that, because I am sure he must have had representations from the president of his own railway, the Canadian National Railways. He must have read the speeches of Mr. Gordon as reported in the newspapers, in which he has pointed out this difficulty. He must have read the remarks made at the annual meetings by Mr. W. A. Mather, chairman of the board of the C.P.R. and Mr. N. R. -better known as "Buck"-Crump, that very

remarkable man who is now president of the C.P.R. They have both pointed out this particular difficulty.
Having made reference to the point I would not want to leave the committee with the feeling that I am advocating throwing the rate-making structure of the railroads completely over and allowing them a complete measure of discretion. We are at a stage where some measure of control is admitted to be, shall we say, necessary in many segments of our economy, and certainly transportation is no exception. But I do suggest that we might allow the railroads more freedom than they have within a certain broad framework.
For example, there should certainly be a ceiling on rates where a railroad enjoys a monopoly on a certain variety of traffic or in connection with transportation in a given area, so that it would not be able to mulct its passengers or those who give it freight to carry. Again there certainly should be a floor in some cases to guard against cutthroat competition designed to drive competing forms of transportation out of business.
Finally I suggest that there might well be certain cases of transportation-western wheat is probably the most outstanding example-where some special measure by the government will be called for if a realistic rate structure is to emerge from the present picture. What that course of action may be is difficult to suggest in the short time at my disposal, but I do suggest, and most strongly, that it is unfair to ask the two railroads of this country to carry a burden which is the direct result of government policy.
It may well be that it is advantageous to Canada as a whole to have a particular rate set for the transportation of western wheat. I think we must take into consideration the position of the western farmer and the need for him to remain economically successful. But having said that, let me suggest that if the transportation rate established for his wheat happens to be uneconomic from the viewpoint of railroad operations, then I think it is unfair to ask and force the railroads to continue to carry that wheat at that uneconomic figure. Some provision should be made for a wider distribution of that burden. Having established a given policy in respect to the carriage of a given commodity the government should accept responsibility for the results of that policy, and not expect the railroads to underwrite it.
No later than tonight we have this article appearing in the Ottawa Journal:
Increasing Rail Freight Rates
The board of transport commissioners announced today it plans to grant the railways shortly an

interim increase in freight rates subject to review next fall. The amount was not specified.
I suggest to you that when you have a business running into the hundreds of millions of dollars-if my memory serves me rightly the gross last year of the C.N.R. was some $600 million-it is rather difficult when it has to go to the board of transport commissioners and get a temporary across the board increase which has no relationship to specific problems and which may be revoked in the fall. Earlier there was reference to the government doing business like a peanut stand, and I suggest that the temporary fixing up of a situation like this is again a reflection of a peanut stand mentality rather than a $600 million mentality.
Finally I should like to quote in summary an article which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of May 25, 1955. In this editorial they say:
It would seem that the railway problem is not just a Canadian problem; it is a North American problem. It is caused by the same thing; overregulation of the railways in an age when they are under severe competition from other means of transport. And for this there would seem to be only one cure.
As the report to the president says: "Adjustment of regulatory programs and policies to these competitive facts is long overdue".
For the benefit of those who may read Hansard or who are listening, may I say that the report to the president refers to a report of a committee set up by President Einsenhower.
There are a number of items which could be taken up under the estimates, but for a moment I should like to touch upon one item which reflects an historical situation which is now due for a change. I refer to the provision of private railway cars for the use of members of the government. This originated many years ago. At that time they were four in number, and probably there was ample justification for their existence. Certainly we did not have air transport at that time, nor did we have the high quality of ordinary rail transport which is available today.
However, over the years and particularly in the last few years we have reached the stage where air transport is the normal method of transport for senior executives. Many corporations have their own private planes. The government has a fleet of private planes which they use day in and day out for the transportation of ministers from one point in Canada to another. Let me say at once that I have no objection to the use of these aeroplanes for that purpose when the end purpose is proper government business.
Despite the fact that ministers have taken to the air in large numbers, we find that no
Supply-Transport
one has yet got around to doing anything about this fleet of private railway cars. The same four cars which they have had over the years are still being kept up with a staff of seven people. The estimate this year is $56,240 for their operation. I suggest that we may need one or perhaps two of these cars only. The Prime Minister on occasion may need that type of transportation. Visiting dignitaries may require that the car be put at their disposal. There may be occasions on which a minister going into a particular part of the country to do business needs to take his travelling hotel along with him and park it on a siding. I am not averse to operating a limited number of these cars, but I suggest that the retention of the four of them as at the present time is a completely unwarranted waste of the taxpayers' money.
Furthermore I suggest that the existence of the cars, lying there idle a good deal of the time, leads the ministers sometimes down unfortunate paths. We had the case, originally denied and then admitted by the Minister of Transport, in which he used one of them to whip down to Montreal and address a political meeting immediately upon his arrival. He did not need the car, and that is obvious from the fact that the next day he came back in an ordinary train, the Canadian.
We have had other cases. Last year, I remember, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration had occasion to travel from one end of Canada to the other with the Minister of Fisheries, one of them at least accompanied by his family, in one of these private cars, for a holiday trip plus a little bit of business on the west coast. These are the devious paths down which people will be led when you leave a little temptation in their way. I suggest that when you have a luxurious private railway car on a siding just waiting to be used, somebody is going to use it and perhaps even take it down to his summer home and park it down there for a few days as a means of transportation. That is costing the taxpayers money. It is not necessary, and it should be cut out.
I see you rising, Mr. Chairman, so I shall take up the other questions further on in the estimates.

I wish to make a few brief remarks on this first item. I shall have a few things to say on one or two of the other items as they come before us.
I understand that the public works department builds wharves and other structures in navigable waters. I am told that the Department of Transport's function is to

Supply-Transport
administer those wharves and certain other structures and supervise them after construction. Before proceeding with the few remarks I wish to make, I want to say that I have every respect for and confidence in the minister's engineer in Victoria, who I think is doing an excellent job, but in my opinion he has a very large district to cover and personally I think he requires more staff. Particularly owing to the development of the interior, I think it is necessary that a senior official of the department, like the district agent in Victoria, have the opportunity himself to visit wharves and certain localities when problems arise and not have to depend in all cases on the report, say, of the junior official of another department.
Up until recent years the arrangements that had been in effect for 50 years were quite satisfactory, but I am speaking now of circumstances of which I have some knowledge. Those intangible arrangements, shall I say, are not sufficient under present conditions, with the development of the logging industry, the lumber industry and the mining industry and the consequent increase in the number of tugs and barges towing logs and things of that sort, and with the necessity for more navigational aids, buoys and that sort of thing. I think there should be a much clearer definition of the responsibilities of the Department of Public Works and the responsibilities of the Department of Transport, and the public should be informed of those definite responsibilities.
I believe that is necessary for the satisfactory supervision of wharves and for the reporting of damage so it can be repaired before greater damage occurs through neglect, and also for the application of the department's regulations without fear or favour, regardless of whether it is a large corporation or a single isolated rancher. Everybody is entitled to be treated alike. I do not believe in the poor man in his little launch being chased away from a government wharf and a corporation being allowed to tie up its vessels for its own purposes. I think there should be some clearer definition of the regulation in that respect.
I realize the difficulties in these isolated cases in the administration of wharves and other structures by the Department of Transsport, but I think the difficulty could be largely overcome by having the R.C.M.P. informed that they can report immediately any damage to these structures and things of that sort, and in other cases perhaps the local postmaster could do this. I have already referred to the considerable damage being done to a wharf in my district because 
the situation was not reported in time to the department. That is all I have to say on that point.
I think it is time we had a revision of the Navigable Waters Protection Act. I find it is an act that is not very effective in many cases. It needs thorough overhauling in the light of modern developments and the changed conditions we find nowadays in industry and on navigable waters. There are clauses in that act with respect to the pollution of navigable waters by sawdust, by slabs, by mill waste and by industrial enterprise. So far as I know, I have never heard of any industry being reported in 50 years as a result of the violation of that act. There again I think the whole act needs overhauling and amending so that these responsibilities are defined as between the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport and so there is control over this pollution of waters.
This was a minor matter until recent years but now, with the great increase in the lumber industry and other industries, it is becoming a serious matter. It has not developed serious proportions to date, but unless there is some strict application of the law in the near future these things will develop and become very serious in the years to come.
I also think it is necessary to have a clearer definition of the responsibility for the renting of space around wharves for gas stations, boat service stations and things of that sort. The department should have a closer check on the driving of piles in navigable waters, and the placing of obstructions in waters by companies or individuals. I am not at all blaming the officials. As I have said before the circumstances have changed, and I am quite certain that the district engineer or district agent for the minister's department in British Columbia needs an addition to his staff so that some senior officials will have an opportunity to get around the province more frequently than they are at present able to do. I think it is particularly necessary that there be a definition of the responsibilities of the two departments and an application of the law in all cases without fear or favour.

speechtext:
I should like at this time to take a few minutes to make two or three observations, and I hope that in making his reply the minister will be favourable to the comments I wish to make at this time.
I do not know whether or not it has been brought to the attention of the minister but it has been brought to my attention on different occasions that a particular situation exists with regard to the pensions of some

of the employees of the Canadian National Railways. Some of these men are getting on in years. We might say that they are in the sunset of life. In the years between 1930 and 1940 a few of them were laid off through no fault of their own and were not credited with pension rights during those years. I believe they are willing to contribute their payments to the pension fund for the time they were laid off. At that time they were willing and ready to go back to work whenever they were called.
I believe it is very unfair to these men to have these years of credit deducted under their pension scheme. I believe they should be eligible for superannuation without these years being deducted. I hope the minister will give the matter very serious consideration. I do not believe there are too many of these men. There are some in the Brockville district in the constituency I represent, and I presume there are a few more across Canada.
I have another problem about which I have spoken before. I believe I spoke of it first three years ago and have brought it up on a couple of occasions since. I refer to the situation in the city of Brockville with respect to the railway station and crossing the railway tracks. I believe the president of the C.N.R., Mr. Gordon, journeyed to Brockville last summer and made an inspection of the conditions that exist there. I did not know of his visit until afterwards; apparently it is the policy not to inform opposition members of such visits. However, I was wondering whether the minister cojild inform me what decision the president of the C.N.R. had made on his visit to Brockville, or if he has made a decision yet.
It is a burning issue so far as the people of Brockville are concerned, not only the residents of Brockville but the community at large and also visitors to the city. The railway lines completely block off two of the main arteries coming into the city from the north. In addition, passengers leaving trains have to travel a long distance back to the station. When the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace was speaking about private cars I was wondering whether it would not be a good idea to put the private cars on the siding and bring the passengers who get off trains from the east or west to the station. There is also a long wait for passenger cars, especially when freight trains are going through, and it is very tedious for the passengers.
If there should be a fire and the fire reels were held up at the crossing, think of the additional damage that might be caused by having to wait for only a few minutes. Then there is the matter of ambulances going to
Supply-Transport
the hospital. I am not quite sure whether I have mentioned this to the house before, but some four or five years ago an ambulance was going to the hospital with an emergency case and was held up for quite some time at the crossing, so long that it did not arrive at the hospital in time. However, I am glad to say that the mother and child are doing fine.
What we greatly need is a subway and a new station. The station is very old and is one that would be appropriate for a little village. We need a subway very badly at that particular point. There are two large public schools on the north side of the town and the children have to cross the railroad tracks. I plead with the minister to do something about this matter. In fact I hope within the next few days to crave his indulgence so that I may have an interview with him for a few minutes in order to go over the whole situation with him.
We are greatly in need of better and safer railway accommodation in the heart of Brockville. Brockville is growing very rapidly to the north and it will only be a short time until the railroad will be in the very centre of the city, which will be most inconvenient if the present situation goes on. When the new by-pass highway, No. 401, is built to the north of the city the main road leading from that highway will cross these tracks, and it is doubly necessary that some provision be made for accommodating that traffic in the next two or three years.
I plead with the minister to do something to alleviate the serious situation we have there. It has been spoken of many times by other members of the house who have been travelling through Brockville and have had to change trains there to come to Ottawa. Many members of the house have said that it is a very undesirable situation. I hope the minister will give very serious consideration not only to the question of the employees and their pension plan but also to the need of a new station and a subway at Brockville.
